flashcards.q: What makes a decision "architectural"?
flashcards.a: It takes a lot of time, money and risk to change later — like the data model or the public API contract.
flashcards.more: A decision isn't measured by how big or technical it looks, but by what it costs to change. You can repaint a house or swap the shutters as often as you like, but changing the foundation means demolishing it. An architect's job is to recognize the software foundations and spend the most time there.

flashcards.q: Which three questions show whether a decision will be costly to change?
flashcards.a: How much stands on it? Has data piled up? Does anyone outside your control use it?
flashcards.more: The first question measures how far the shock of a change will spread. The second measures how much data must move into a new mould. The third measures whether you can change it alone or must wait for someone else. The more "yes" answers, the more the decision behaves like a foundation.

flashcards.q: What are the four familiar architectural decisions?
flashcards.a: Database choice, data model, service boundaries and the public API contract.
flashcards.more: All four involve either stored data or an outside dependency, so changing them later takes weeks or months. When you face one, stop, think of at least two alternatives and write down your reason. Language, framework and the login method often belong in this group too.

flashcards.q: What is bikeshedding?
flashcards.a: Arguing at length over trivial, easy topics while rushing hard, expensive decisions through.
flashcards.more: Everyone understands the easy topics, so everyone has an opinion; on hard ones people stay quiet. So a design review spends 40 minutes on button colors and the data model passes in five minutes. The cure is to ask before the discussion: "What will it cost to change this later?"

flashcards.q: Why is changing a public API contract so hard?
flashcards.a: Because the clients aren't in your hands: old mobile apps and partner systems change on their own schedule, not yours.
flashcards.more: You can change your own code in a single deploy. But an old app on a user's phone will keep asking for the old fields for months. So when you change a contract, old and new must run side by side for a long time. More in [[api/contracts-versioning/renamed-field|contracts and versioning]].

flashcards.q: Why does stored data make a decision expensive?
flashcards.a: Changing code isn't enough — millions of rows must move into a new shape, without taking the live system down.
flashcards.more: On day one the tables are empty, so changing the data model takes a minute. Two years later the same change needs a migration, step-by-step data moves and verification. That's why a data-model mistake gets costlier the later it's caught.

flashcards.q: What's the danger of returning a Doctrine entity directly as JSON?
flashcards.a: Your table columns become API fields: renaming a column breaks clients, and secret columns can leak out.
flashcards.more: A cheap decision (a column name) quietly becomes expensive because everyone outside starts depending on it. The fix is a separate response class (a DTO) holding only the fields you are willing to promise to the outside.

flashcards.q: How should you split your time across a feature's decisions?
flashcards.a: List every decision with its cost of change: minutes, days, weeks, months. Spend review time only on weeks and months.
flashcards.more: A feature usually holds many decisions, but only two or three behave like foundations. Write two alternatives and a reason for those and have them reviewed. One person can decide the rest and move on, since fixing a mistake there is cheap.

flashcards.q: How do you keep a cheap decision cheap?
flashcards.a: Put a thin layer between the inside and the outside promise: a response class, an interface or an adapter.
flashcards.more: When many things lean directly on one thing, it gets hard to move. The layer in between absorbs the shock: if a column or a vendor changes inside, only one class in that layer changes and nobody outside notices. The price is an extra class and some mapping code, so skip it for screens only your own team uses.

flashcards.q: What is a two-way door decision?
flashcards.a: One that is easy and cheap to reverse if it turns out wrong, such as turning on a feature flag or changing a banner color.
flashcards.more: Long discussion on such a decision is wasted time. Let one person decide and move on; if it's wrong, you can come back and correct it. Speed is the real advantage here.

flashcards.q: What is a one-way door decision?
flashcards.a: One that can't be undone once made, or whose reversal is hugely costly, such as deleting data or removing a public API field.
flashcards.more: Stop on these: consider alternatives, write down the risks, get a second person to look. A mistake is costly and permanent, so a few extra hours of thought pay off.

flashcards.q: What question tells a two-way door from a one-way door?
flashcards.a: "If I'm wrong, how do I get back, and at what cost?" "One click" means two-way; "I can't" means one-way.
flashcards.more: The question is about the cost of going back, not the size of the decision. A small migration can be one-way (dropping a column), while a big-looking job can be a two-way door (a new checkout behind a flag).

flashcards.q: What goes wrong if you change code and drop a column in the same deploy?
flashcards.a: If the new code has a bug, going back to the old code doesn't help, because the column is gone. Your way back is cut off.
flashcards.more: Rollback works for code, not for data. So the drop has to come after the code change, in its own deploy, with a backup.

flashcards.q: What are the four steps of an expand-contract migration?
flashcards.a: Expand (add the new), migrate (copy the data), switch (code reads the new), contract (drop the old).
flashcards.more: Each step is its own deploy. Only the last step is one-way; in the other three the old column stays intact, so you can return to the earlier state at any time.

flashcards.q: Before the final DROP COLUMN, what check proves no data would be lost?
flashcards.a: Count rows where the old column has a value but the new one is NULL. It must return 0, and you need a backup.
flashcards.more: In the example: `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customer WHERE phone IS NOT NULL AND mobile_number IS NULL;`. A non-zero result means some numbers exist only in the old column, which is exactly how Sarah's team lost theirs.

flashcards.q: What does expand-contract cost, and when is it overkill?
flashcards.a: Four deploys instead of one, plus a while of double writes. Overkill for scratch data or a tiny table you can rebuild in minutes.
flashcards.more: The price buys a safe way back. For any column that holds real customer data it is worth it; for a dev database it is not.

flashcards.q: What does turning a feature flag off NOT undo?
flashcards.a: Whatever the new path already wrote or sent. The flag brings back the old code path, not the data or the emails.
flashcards.more: If the new checkout charged 40 customers before you flipped the flag, those 40 charges stay. Use flags for risky code, and still plan how to fix what the new path already did.

flashcards.q: What are two common ways to turn a one-way door into a two-way one?
flashcards.a: Keep external things behind an interface, and keep the new path behind a feature flag.
flashcards.more: With an interface, switching vendor is the job of one class. With a flag, if the new path misbehaves you flip the switch and the old path is back. Both cost a little effort up front and save a big cost later.

flashcards.q: Why shouldn't a feature flag stay around for long?
flashcards.a: An old flag keeps two code paths alive and adds complexity. So give every flag a removal date.
flashcards.more: A flag is a temporary ladder. When the job is done, delete one of the two paths and remove the flag. Otherwise, in time nobody knows what each flag does, and that's the new clutter.

flashcards.q: What is tech debt?
flashcards.a: A shortcut taken in today's rush, whose price is paid later as extra time and risk on every change.
flashcards.more: A shortcut saves time now, but until the code is fixed every new job goes slower. That slowdown is the interest. Fix the debt and the interest stops.

flashcards.q: What are the "principal" and "interest" of tech debt?
flashcards.a: Principal: the work needed now to fix the shortcut. Interest: the extra cost on every change until it's fixed.
flashcards.more: A small principal can carry big interest if the code is touched often. A big principal can carry little interest if nobody touches the code. Measuring interest is what helps you decide the order of repayment.

flashcards.q: What separates deliberate debt from inadvertent debt?
flashcards.a: Deliberate debt is written down and comes with a repayment plan; inadvertent debt piles up without anyone knowing.
flashcards.more: The first is a tactic, because business races against time. The second comes from lack of knowledge or neglect. So learning and code review are the main protection against inadvertent debt.

flashcards.q: What are the three conditions for good tech debt?
flashcards.a: You know what was cut, you know the interest, and there's a repayment date and an owner.
flashcards.more: If any of the three is missing, the debt gets out of control. The third is the one most often forgotten, which is why "we'll fix it later" never comes.

flashcards.q: What should an entry in a debt register contain?
flashcards.a: What, why it was taken, the interest, the way to repay, an owner and a due date.
flashcards.more: A one-page entry is enough. Add a marker with the ticket number in the code and one grep finds every debt. A glance at the register each sprint shows which debts have passed their date.

flashcards.q: What is the boy-scout rule?
flashcards.a: Leave any file you touch a little cleaner than you found it, such as naming a magic number.
flashcards.more: This means big refactoring doesn't need separate time, and the most-touched code gets cleaned the most. The condition: the change must be small and safe, and tests must exist.

flashcards.q: Why is copy-pasted code expensive?
flashcards.a: Every later change must be made in each copy, and a forgotten copy keeps the old behavior: a bug that only shows up there.
flashcards.more: In the Black Friday example, the tax update reached `CheckoutService` but not the copy, so Black Friday orders were taxed at the old rate. Each extra copy multiplies this risk.

flashcards.q: How do you safely merge two near-identical classes?
flashcards.a: First write a test that records both classes' current outputs, then merge, turning the one real difference into a small injected strategy.
flashcards.more: The test is your safety net. The strategy keeps the difference (such as the Black Friday discount) out of the shared code, so the shared rules live in one place.

flashcards.q: Why is "stop everything and rewrite" a poor way to repay debt?
flashcards.a: Old code holds years of unwritten rules and bug fixes. A rewrite drops many of them and runs longer than planned.
flashcards.more: Repay in small installments instead: clean what you touch, reserve some time each sprint, and start with the highest-interest debt.

flashcards.q: How much of a sprint is reasonable to set aside for debt?
flashcards.a: Many teams reserve roughly 15-20 percent. The number varies by team; being regular is what matters.
flashcards.more: A fixed share means debt repayment doesn't get dropped every time business pressure rises. Even if the share is small, keep it in every sprint, because regular small installments are far safer than one big repayment.

flashcards.q: What problem do microservices actually solve?
flashcards.a: An organizational one: letting many teams change and deploy independently without waiting on each other.
flashcards.more: You don't need microservices for tidy code or for speed; a modular monolith gives you that too. A small team doesn't have the problem, so the solution just becomes extra weight.

flashcards.q: What are the four real costs of microservices?
flashcards.a: Slow, failure-prone network calls; separate deploys and logs; broken transactions; and the complexity of running the whole system.
flashcards.more: A method call inside one process is almost free and doesn't fail. A call between services brings timeouts, retries and partial failures. Once data is split across several databases, one transaction can't keep everything consistent.

flashcards.q: A request passes through 5 services, each 99.9% reliable. How often does it fail?
flashcards.a: About 5 times in 1,000 (0.999 to the power 5 is about 0.995), against 1 in 1,000 for a single app. Every extra hop adds a chance to fail.
flashcards.more: That is 5 failed orders for every 1,000 instead of 1, with no bug anywhere, just arithmetic. Add timeouts and retries and the code to handle it grows too. Inside one app, a method call has no such odds.

flashcards.q: What is a modular monolith?
flashcards.a: One app and one deploy, with firm business-capability modules inside, each with its own public API and its own data.
flashcards.more: It keeps the simplicity of a monolith (one deploy, method calls, one transaction) and adds the tidy boundaries of microservices. And if the boundaries are right, turning a module into a separate service later is easy.

flashcards.q: What is a distributed monolith?
flashcards.a: An app split into services but coupled so tightly that changing one means deploying them all together.
flashcards.more: It has all the costs of microservices and none of the benefit of independence. It usually comes from wrong boundaries or from everyone sharing one database. A modular monolith with real boundaries is far better.

flashcards.q: How should one module talk to another?
flashcards.a: Through the other module's public `Api` interface, holding only its ID rather than its entity.
flashcards.more: If you use another module's Doctrine relation or call its repository directly, the boundary exists only in name. With an interface and IDs, the rest of the code stays nearly the same even if the module later becomes a separate service. Deptrac can guard this in CI.

flashcards.q: What does a modular monolith cost you?
flashcards.a: Discipline: nothing stops a shortcut across modules unless a tool such as Deptrac fails the build. You also can't scale or deploy one module alone.
flashcards.more: The boundaries are only folders until something enforces them. Run Deptrac in CI so a `ManyToOne` into another module fails the build. And because it is one deploy, a module that needs ten servers drags the rest along.

flashcards.q: By what rule should service boundaries be drawn?
flashcards.a: By business capability and data ownership, so that each service is the sole owner of its data.
flashcards.more: Splitting by technical layer (Controller, Database) is wrong, because every feature passes through all the layers. Splitting by business capability keeps most features in one place. More in [[thinking/ddd/two-languages|DDD and bounded contexts]].

flashcards.q: When is it reasonable to turn a module into a separate service?
flashcards.a: When a separate team wants to deploy independently, it needs separate scaling, and the boundary has been stable for months.
flashcards.more: "A big app" or "everyone does it" aren't reasons. You also need people to carry the cost of running a service (monitoring, CI, data reconciliation). If these conditions aren't met, staying with a modular monolith is better.

flashcards.q: What are the separate jobs of the controller, service and repository?
flashcards.a: The controller handles HTTP, the service runs business rules, and the repository fetches and stores data.
flashcards.more: Like the waiter, cook and storekeeper in a restaurant. A change in one (say, HTTP to a queue handler) doesn't touch the others, and each can be tested separately.

flashcards.q: Which way do dependencies run between layers?
flashcards.a: Top to bottom. The controller knows the service and the service knows the repository, never the reverse.
flashcards.more: When a lower layer knows the one above (say, a `Request` inside a service), the same rule can't be used elsewhere (a console command, a queue). Go one step further and you can invert dependencies entirely; that is [[thinking/hexagonal/wired-to-everything|hexagonal]].

flashcards.q: Why is a fat controller a problem?
flashcards.a: The business rules are trapped in the controller, so you can't reuse them, test them separately or change them safely.
flashcards.more: The same rule has to be copied, and the copies drift apart over time. Move the rule into a service and one change updates every place at once.

flashcards.q: A discount rule is needed in three places. How do you keep them in step?
flashcards.a: Write it once in its own class, such as `DiscountPolicy`, and have the checkout, the other API and the admin page all call it.
flashcards.more: With three copies, a change that updates two leaves the third showing an old price: $102 at checkout, $108 on the admin page for the same $120 first order. With one class, one edit updates every caller and the rule gets its own test.

flashcards.q: Why is it wrong for a service to hold a `Request` object?
flashcards.a: It ties the business rule to HTTP, so the rule can't be used from a console command or a queue handler.
flashcards.more: The controller pulls the needed values out of the `Request` and gives the service plain values or a DTO. The service then doesn't know who is calling it: a browser, a command or a test.

flashcards.q: What is the strangler fig technique?
flashcards.a: Put a router in front of the old app, move paths to new code one at a time, and finally delete the old code.
flashcards.more: The name comes from a tree that grows up another tree and slowly takes its place. It carries far less risk than rewriting the whole system in one go, because every step is small and reversible.

flashcards.q: What are the four steps of the strangler fig?
flashcards.a: Put a router in front, rewrite one small path, run both side by side and compare, then shift traffic and delete the old code.
flashcards.more: For the first path, choose one with low risk and few dependencies (a report, say). In the last step, don't forget to delete the old code, or both systems keep running forever.

flashcards.q: What breaks if you rename a column while the old and new apps share a table?
flashcards.a: The old app still reads the old name and fails at once. Add the new column, backfill, switch the new app, and drop the old one only after the old app is gone.
flashcards.more: This is expand and contract. Adding a nullable column breaks nobody. The drop is the one step you cannot undo, so it comes last, when no old code reads the column.

flashcards.q: How does the new app know who is logged in during a strangler migration?
flashcards.a: The browser sends one cookie to both apps. The new app asks the old one, over a private endpoint, who that cookie belongs to. Login moves last.
flashcards.more: The router puts both apps on one domain, so no second login is needed. The private endpoint must never be reachable from the internet, and its answer can be cached briefly so the old app does not become the bottleneck.

flashcards.q: What is an anti-corruption layer for?
flashcards.a: It confines the old system's odd names and formats to one translator class so the new code stays clean.
flashcards.more: The translator turns the old `st = A` into the new code's `active: true`. When the old system changes, only the translator class changes. It is a form of the hexagonal adapter.

flashcards.q: Why is rewriting a legacy system in one go risky?
flashcards.a: Old code holds years of hidden rules that get lost in a rewrite, and the work takes far longer than estimated.
flashcards.more: Throughout the rewrite the old system keeps changing, so the new one is always behind: a plan of 6 months easily becomes 14. Moving step by step means each step is checked with real users.

flashcards.q: What is a stateless server?
flashcards.a: A server that remembers nothing about the user between requests. All memory lives outside it.
flashcards.more: That means any server can handle any request. Adding servers, replacing them and swapping in a fresh one for a dead one all become easy.

flashcards.q: What happens when session files sit on each server's own disk and there are several servers?
flashcards.a: When the user hits a different server it can't find their session, so they suddenly appear logged out.
flashcards.more: Disk sessions work fine on one server, but break once a load balancer splits the requests. The fix is to keep sessions in Redis or the database, where every server reads the same ledger.

flashcards.q: Why are sticky sessions not a good fix?
flashcards.a: If that server dies or is redeployed its users lose their sessions, and load is not spread evenly.
flashcards.more: Sticky sessions hide the problem rather than solve it. The real fix is to move state outside the servers, so it no longer matters which server gets the request.

flashcards.q: With several servers, where should uploaded files be stored?
flashcards.a: In object storage (S3-style), not on a server's local disk. The database holds only the file's key.
flashcards.more: Files on a local disk are invisible to other servers and disappear when the server dies. In Symfony, Flysystem gives you one interface where you can swap the local and S3 adapters through config alone.

flashcards.q: In Flysystem, how does `$uploadsStorage` get connected to S3?
flashcards.a: A storage named `uploads.storage` in flysystem.yaml is autowired as `FilesystemOperator $uploadsStorage`. Its adapter decides S3 or local.
flashcards.more: Use `adapter: aws` in prod and `adapter: local` in dev under the same name, and the upload code never changes. The S3 client is a service the config points to. S3 reads and writes are network calls, so they are slower than a local disk.

flashcards.q: What does 1,000 simultaneous users do to a database behind serverless?
flashcards.a: About 1,000 instances start, each opens its own connection, and the database hits its limit. A pooler or proxy in front fixes it.
flashcards.more: A small MySQL server accepts about 150 connections by default. RDS Proxy or PgBouncer keeps a few real connections and lends them to the instances. It is one more piece to run and monitor.

flashcards.q: What does Symfony need to store sessions in Redis?
flashcards.a: Set `framework.session.handler_id` to the Redis DSN, for example `%env(REDIS_URL)%`.
flashcards.more: No code changes, only config. All servers read and write sessions in the same Redis. Redis is now a dependency too, so think about its backups and availability.

flashcards.q: What is serverless?
flashcards.a: A model where the platform runs the servers, your code runs when requests arrive, and you pay for what you use.
flashcards.more: The servers still exist, you just don't run them. When no requests come in, instances are shut down; when they do, new ones start. Your code must be stateless, because an instance can be stopped or recreated at any moment.

flashcards.q: What is a cold start?
flashcards.a: The wait for a new instance to boot on the first request after a quiet period, which makes that request slow.
flashcards.more: This is when the code is downloaded and the runtime and framework start up. Later requests reach a warm instance and are fast. It is a problem where every response must be consistently quick.

flashcards.q: What kind of work suits serverless best?
flashcards.a: Small, irregular or event-driven jobs: webhooks, file processing, nightly tasks. Not constant heavy traffic.
flashcards.more: For work that sits idle most of the time and then arrives in bursts, pay-per-use is cheap. In a system that is busy all day, a fixed-price server or container is usually cheaper and more predictable.

flashcards.q: What is a quality attribute?
flashcards.a: Not what a system does but how well it does it: speed, availability, security, maintainability, cost.
flashcards.more: The same feature can be slow or fast, safe or unsafe. These qualities steer architecture decisions because they are the hardest things to change later.

flashcards.q: What are the five main quality attributes?
flashcards.a: Performance (speed), availability, security, maintainability and cost.
flashcards.more: There are more, such as scalability, observability and usability, but these five start most discussions. The key point is that each has a price, and that price is paid out of another quality.

flashcards.q: What goes up when you raise availability?
flashcards.a: Cost and complexity, because you need extra servers, replicas, a load balancer and data syncing.
flashcards.more: To stay up when one thing dies, you must keep a spare. That spare needs its own maintenance, monitoring and data syncing.

flashcards.q: Why is "the system should be fast" a bad requirement?
flashcards.a: It can't be measured. Without knowing how fast and under what conditions, nobody can say when it's done.
flashcards.more: A good requirement has a scenario, a measure and a target: "with 100 people checking out at once, p95 latency stays under 300ms." Then a load test can really verify it.

flashcards.q: What does p95 latency mean?
flashcards.a: The time within which 95 out of every 100 requests finish. The other 5 are slower.
flashcards.more: An average hides slow requests. p95 or p99 shows how bad the worst experiences are, and those slow requests are exactly what users remember. More in [[observability/metrics-slos/average-lies|metrics and SLOs]].

flashcards.q: How much downtime a month does 99.9% availability allow?
flashcards.a: About 43 minutes. At 99% it is about 7 hours, and at 99.99% about 4 minutes.
flashcards.more: Each extra nine cuts the allowed downtime to a tenth, but the cost grows many times over. So first find out what an hour of downtime costs the business.

flashcards.q: How do you decide whether one more "nine" of availability is worth it?
flashcards.a: Price the downtime it removes in lost money, and compare that with what the extra nine costs to run.
flashcards.more: Example: if an hour of downtime costs a shop $1,200, going from 99.9% to 99.99% removes about 39 minutes a month, roughly $780. If the automatic failover costs more than that every month, it isn't worth it yet.

flashcards.q: Why can't all quality attributes get equal priority?
flashcards.a: Raising one lowers another. So pick the two most important for the business first, then put a bar under the rest.
flashcards.more: A money app puts security and availability first; a personal blog puts cost and maintainability first. Writing down why you chose them is the real work, because everyone will later ask "why this and not that?"

flashcards.q: What is back-of-envelope estimation?
flashcards.a: A quick calculation with rounded numbers that tells you the scale of a system: 10, 10 thousand or 10 million.
flashcards.more: The goal is not precision but catching 10x errors. A few minutes of math shows whether one server is enough, whether you need sharding, and which part deserves the most thought.

flashcards.q: How do you work out average QPS?
flashcards.a: Total requests per day divided by 86,400 (quickly, divide by 100,000).
flashcards.more: For example, 5 million requests a day / 100,000 is about 50 QPS. This is only an average, so you must apply a peak factor before sizing servers.

flashcards.q: Why size servers for peak QPS instead of the average?
flashcards.a: Because systems break in the busiest hour. Build for the average and the site goes down on sale day or holiday night.
flashcards.more: The factor is usually 3 to 10x, depending on the business. Look at the busiest hour in your own access log to find the real figure.

flashcards.q: Roughly what QPS is 1 million requests a day?
flashcards.a: About 12 QPS. So 10 million requests a day is only around 120 QPS.
flashcards.more: Many people assume millions of requests means a huge server fleet. But spread over a whole day, the number is much smaller. Divide before you panic.

flashcards.q: Roughly how long do a RAM read, an SSD read and a network round trip take?
flashcards.a: RAM ≈ 100 nanoseconds, random SSD read ≈ 0.1 ms, round trip within one data center ≈ 0.5 ms.
flashcards.more: Going from RAM to SSD is about a thousand times slower, and a network round trip is a few times slower again. That is why caches live in RAM, and why many small service calls add up to a lot of network time.

flashcards.q: What else must a storage estimate include beyond the raw data?
flashcards.a: Indexes and replicas. In practice you need 2-3x the raw data.
flashcards.more: Even if the raw data is 120 GB, indexes take extra space and replicas multiply the copies. Forget them and a full-disk alarm arrives out of nowhere.

flashcards.q: How should you report an estimate?
flashcards.a: As a rounded number or a range, such as "about 3" or "2 to 5", with the assumptions written next to it.
flashcards.more: Writing "57.3 servers" is false precision. A range plus a list of assumptions lets anyone see how much the answer moves if an assumption changes. That makes the discussion easier.

flashcards.q: The sum gives 3 servers, so why does the package-tracking cost line count 5 machines?
flashcards.a: The 3 are app servers only. The database and Redis each need a machine too, so 3 + 1 + 1 = 5 machines.
flashcards.more: A cost line must count every machine, not just the ones the QPS sum produced. At $200 per machine (an assumed price), 5 machines come to about $1,000 a month.

flashcards.q: After the estimate, what comes next: guess more or measure?
flashcards.a: Measure whichever assumption changes the answer most, for example with a load test or the access log.
flashcards.more: Start with an estimate, but measure wherever you can. You can assume a server handles 150 QPS, but a 30-minute load test gives you the real number.

flashcards.q: What is a complexity budget?
flashcards.a: The limit on how much complexity a team can handle at once. Every new technology spends from this budget.
flashcards.more: A team's attention and time are limited. Every new database, queue or language brings learning, running and fixing. When the budget runs out, the team can no longer build features and only tends machinery. So before adding anything, check whether what you already have can do the job.

flashcards.q: What does "boring technology" mean?
flashcards.a: Mature, widely used technology whose failure modes and fixes are already well known, such as PostgreSQL.
flashcards.more: Boring doesn't mean old or weak. It means few surprises: errors have known fixes, experienced people are easy to find, and the tooling is mature. New technology hides unknown problems that are found only in production.

flashcards.q: What ongoing costs does a new technology bring?
flashcards.a: Learning, running (deploy, monitoring, backup), upgrading (versions, patches), fixing when it breaks, and finally the cost of removing it.
flashcards.more: Installing is a one-time cost, but these five continue for as long as the technology stays. Most are paid in team time, not money, so they don't show up on a bill. If the technology lives in one person's head, the whole team is in trouble when they leave.

flashcards.q: What should you build yourself, and what should you buy?
flashcards.a: Build what sets your business apart. Buy what everyone needs in the same way (payments, SMS, email).
flashcards.more: Building takes time and attention, so spend it where the business is really strong, its core domain. For things everyone needs, others have spent years making good solutions, and rebuilding them wastes time. For a detailed comparison see [[thinking/build-vs-buy/three-roads|the three roads]].

flashcards.q: Open source software is "free", so where is the cost?
flashcards.a: The license is free, but servers, setup, upgrades, backups, monitoring and fixing problems are all on you.
flashcards.more: It's like a free recipe: the recipe costs nothing, but the shopping, the cooking and any spoiled batch are yours. A self-run open source tool often has a higher total cost than SaaS, because people's time is the most expensive part. Still, with a mature tool and skilled people to run it, it can be the best road.

flashcards.q: What is TCO (total cost of ownership)?
flashcards.a: The total cost of a thing for as long as you keep it: setup + running + people's time + eventually leaving it.
flashcards.more: Deciding by the license or the first month's bill alone is a mistake. A typical TCO covers three years: initial engineer-days, 36 months of bills or servers, maintenance days each month, and the cost of moving away. Add everything up before you compare.

flashcards.q: Which cost does a TCO calculation most often leave out?
flashcards.a: Engineer time: the days spent on setup, learning and monthly maintenance.
flashcards.more: You can see a bill, but people's time never shows up on an invoice. Yet 3 days of maintenance a month, at $500 a day, comes to $54,000 over three years. And the features you couldn't build in that time are a separate loss.

flashcards.q: What is vendor lock-in, and how do you prevent it?
flashcards.a: Depending on a vendor so much that leaving is nearly impossible. Prevent it by putting the vendor behind an interface.
flashcards.more: If a vendor's SDK is spread through your code, then when the vendor raises prices or shuts down, you have to rewrite everything. If business code knows only an interface, a change touches one adapter or config file. Also make sure you can export your data. More: [[thinking/hexagonal/wired-to-everything|ports and adapters]].

flashcards.q: What does hiding a vendor behind an interface cost you?
flashcards.a: A little extra code, and you can use only the features every vendor shares. Skip it for tools you will never swap.
flashcards.more: An interface that fits Twilio and another SMS vendor can offer only plain SMS. A feature that only one vendor has needs its own adapter or a vendor-specific option. So wrap the services most likely to change or turn expensive, such as SMS or payments, and don't wrap a framework you will live with for ten years.

flashcards.q: What should drive the choice of a language and framework?
flashcards.a: What the application needs: workload, correctness, built-in features, integrations, team skills and support length. Not fashion or habit.
flashcards.more: A stack is a tool for a job. Write the job's needs down first, then see which stacks fit. Choosing by fashion or by what the team happens to know pushes the cost to later, when the mismatch shows up as slow delivery or bugs in the parts that matter most.

flashcards.q: What six questions should you answer before choosing a stack?
flashcards.a: Workload shape, correctness needs, built-in features, integration, team and hiring, and support and stability.
flashcards.more: Think of the vehicle: what you carry, how fragile it is, which fittings come with it, which roads it must join, who can drive and repair it, and how long spare parts are made. The answers form a shopping list of properties, not one winning brand.

flashcards.q: What is workload shape?
flashcards.a: What the system mostly does: move big files, wait on other services, apply many rules, or record many small changes safely.
flashcards.more: A video site is mostly bytes moving and background conversion. An insurance system is mostly many small, careful writes under strict rules. The shape tells you which parts of a stack will matter most for the job.

flashcards.q: Why does the web backend language matter less for video streaming?
flashcards.a: The heavy work, converting and delivering video, runs in storage, background workers like ffmpeg and a CDN, not in the web framework.
flashcards.more: The web app mostly accepts uploads and logins, then hands files to object storage and a converter. Viewers stream from a CDN. So many web languages work, and the effort goes into the pipeline, queues and delivery cost instead.

flashcards.q: What needs does an insurance or accounting system put on a stack?
flashcards.a: Exact decimals, strict transactions, an audit trail, access rules, batch jobs and long support, because wrong values become legal problems.
flashcards.more: Money and records must add up to the cent and every change must be traceable. A stack that ships transactions, security, batch and scheduling ready-made lets the team spend its time on the insurance rules instead of the plumbing.

flashcards.q: Why are Spring Boot and .NET common in enterprise accounting and insurance?
flashcards.a: They ship tested transactions, security and batch tools built in, are strongly typed, and have long-term-support releases.
flashcards.more: Spring has declarative `@Transactional`, Spring Security and Spring Batch. .NET has Entity Framework Core, built-in dependency injection and ASP.NET Core Identity. Long support cycles suit systems that live for ten years. This does not make them the only good choice.

flashcards.q: Can Django or Symfony run accounting software?
flashcards.a: Yes. No stack is wrong. Check that the pieces you need exist and are mature, and add and test what is missing.
flashcards.more: Symfony, the stack of this course, ships Doctrine transactions, Security voters, Messenger, Workflow, Lock and Scheduler. Django can use exact decimal fields and database transactions. The honest question is not which language, but who writes and tests each missing piece.

flashcards.q: What is the price of a framework with many built-in features?
flashcards.a: More to learn, more ceremony for small jobs, and a pull toward its ecosystem. It also spends complexity budget.
flashcards.more: The other side is real too. Without built-ins you write transaction handling, permission checks and restartable batches yourself, and bugs there touch money. Choose the price you can pay: for money-heavy work, learning the framework usually costs less than hand-building.

flashcards.q: Why is rewriting a working system into a trendy stack risky?
flashcards.a: It re-creates years of hidden rules, runs two systems for a long time, and often leaves the real, unmeasured problem unfixed.
flashcards.more: Measure first. A slow report may need one index, not a new language. Rewrite only when a measured limit cannot be fixed inside the current stack, for example when it has lost security support. Otherwise you spend the [[thinking/build-vs-buy/too-many-machines|complexity budget]] on a guess.

flashcards.q: What is Conway's Law in one line?
flashcards.a: The structure of a system copies the communication structure of the organization that builds it.
flashcards.more: Code takes the shape of the lines along which teams talk. Three teams usually produce a system in three parts. It isn't a law of nature but an observation that has held many times.

flashcards.q: What goes wrong when you split teams by layer (UI, Backend, DB)?
flashcards.a: Every feature touches every layer, so every feature involves every team. Tickets get handed off and wait.
flashcards.more: Two days of work waits through three teams' queues and becomes three weeks. Each team does its job well, yet it is still slow, because the delay is in the handoffs. The fix is full-stack teams split by business capability.

flashcards.q: What is the inverse Conway maneuver?
flashcards.a: Arrange teams along the architecture you want, so the teams' natural communication produces that architecture.
flashcards.more: Normally the teams come first and the system grows in their mould. Here you reverse the order: draw the boundaries you want, then put an owning team on each. Details: [[thinking/conways-law/inverse-conway|the five steps]].

flashcards.q: How should teams and services be matched?
flashcards.a: Each service or module gets one owning team, and its size stays within what that team can handle.
flashcards.more: When three teams commit to one service, nobody is accountable. When one small team holds eight services, it can run none of them well. Friction grows in both cases.

flashcards.q: How can you write down a module's ownership in code?
flashcards.a: In a CODEOWNERS file, listing the owning team per path, so a pull request on that path can't merge without the owner's review.
flashcards.more: On GitHub or GitLab, writing `/src/Billing/ @shop/billing-team` makes the Billing team an automatic reviewer for any change to Billing code. Ownership stops being talk and becomes something you can see.

flashcards.q: What should you take from another team's module?
flashcards.a: Only the interface or API they publish, never their Doctrine entities or internal classes.
flashcards.more: If you depend on internal classes, your code breaks whenever the owning team changes anything. If you depend on an interface, they can change anything inside as long as the contract holds. That is the whole point of a boundary.

flashcards.q: How do you decide which services to merge when redrawing boundaries?
flashcards.a: List which services each recent feature touched. Services that keep changing together are one boundary: merge them under one owner.
flashcards.more: For example, if coupon, free-delivery and gift-wrap features all changed cart, price and order, those three belong in one Checkout module. The price is real merge work and one shared deploy, so keep a part separate only if it truly needs its own scaling.

flashcards.q: Why does changing only the org chart not help?
flashcards.a: The code boundaries stay as they were. New teams on the old code split keep the friction.
flashcards.more: Conway's Law works both ways: change the teams and the system slowly follows; leave the system alone and the teams drift back to the old shape. A reorganization needs the code boundaries and ownership redrawn too.

flashcards.q: What is evolutionary architecture?
flashcards.a: An architecture that can change in small, safe steps and still keeps its important qualities while it changes.
flashcards.more: The goal is not a perfect design up front; it is to keep change safe. Automated checks run at every step so that a change can't quietly break a rule or a quality.

flashcards.q: What is a fitness function?
flashcards.a: An automated check that measures an architectural quality or rule, reports pass or fail, and runs in CI.
flashcards.more: Examples: "no Doctrine in the Domain" (Deptrac), "no more than 10 queries on the list" (PHPUnit), "p95 of 300ms" (k6). Like a bathroom scale, it tells you the moment a rule is broken.

flashcards.q: What is architecture drift?
flashcards.a: The code slowly, almost silently, moving away from the rules of the real architecture.
flashcards.more: A single shortcut looks harmless, so nobody blocks it in review. But over months they pile up into serious decay. Automated checks are the only reliable prevention.

flashcards.q: What is Deptrac used for?
flashcards.a: You write down which code layer may know which, and CI fails when the rules are broken.
flashcards.more: deptrac.yaml describes layers such as Domain, Application and Infrastructure and the permissions between them. `vendor/bin/deptrac analyse` reads dependencies without running the code and checks them against the rules. PHPat and PHPArkitect are similar alternatives.

flashcards.q: Why does a Deptrac setup need a layer for the Doctrine library?
flashcards.a: Doctrine lives in vendor/, outside src/. Unless you name it as a layer, Deptrac cannot see a Doctrine import inside Domain.
flashcards.more: Add a layer with a `classNameRegex` collector for `Doctrine\.*`, and give Domain an empty rule (`Domain: ~`). Then one Doctrine import in a Domain class fails the build. Keep the mapping outside the class, for example in an XML file under Infrastructure.

flashcards.q: A developer adds Doctrine attributes to a Domain class and Deptrac fails. What is the fix?
flashcards.a: Keep the Domain class plain and move the mapping out, for example into an XML mapping file in Infrastructure.
flashcards.more: Do not switch the guard off. The rule exists so the Domain stays free of Doctrine. Old violations that cannot be fixed today go into a baseline file; new ones are blocked.

flashcards.q: What does a fitness function cost, and which rules should you not guard this way?
flashcards.a: Upkeep, and a flaky one teaches people to ignore red builds. Guard rules worth defending; leave taste (naming, spacing) to a style tool.
flashcards.more: Start with two or three rules that protect something expensive to lose: layer boundaries, a speed budget, security. Every extra check is code someone must maintain.

flashcards.q: What is a performance budget?
flashcards.a: A speed limit (say p95 of 300ms, or 10 queries) that fails CI when exceeded.
flashcards.more: Once an app gets slow it is hard to win the speed back, because everyone gets used to it. With a budget, every change has to answer to the limit. In CI, measure stable things like query count instead of time, and your tests won't be flaky.

flashcards.q: What is the last responsible moment?
flashcards.a: The final point after which not deciding starts to cost you. Until then, you can postpone the decision.
flashcards.more: The later you decide, the more information you have. So decide hard-to-change things just before that moment. But "later" must not be open-ended: write down in advance which measured number will trigger the decision.

flashcards.q: What must you write down when you postpone a decision?
flashcards.a: A trigger: the measured number or event that will make you decide.
flashcards.more: For example: "if we pass 1000 messages a minute (about 17 a second) or the queue lag exceeds a minute, we move to Redis". Without a trigger, postponing is really avoidance, and the problem arrives like a fire.

flashcards.q: What is a design reviewer's real job?
flashcards.a: To pull out the author's unstated assumptions and the failure paths, not just to back the happy path.
flashcards.more: A design document almost always describes the happy path. A reviewer asks like an engineer, "what if the pipe bursts?", because they didn't build the thing and so their eyes are on the bad days.

flashcards.q: What are the four core questions of a design review?
flashcards.a: What if it fails? What if it arrives twice? What if it is slow? What if we run it again (retry)?
flashcards.more: You can ask these four at every arrow or step. Behind them sit timeouts, idempotency, queues and safe retries. More in [[thinking/design-review/four-questions|the four-question checklist]].

flashcards.q: What is a good answer to "what if it arrives twice?"
flashcards.a: Make the job idempotent: running the same job several times gives the same result, for example with an Idempotency-Key or a unique constraint.
flashcards.more: Double clicks, retries and messages delivered twice all really happen. With an idempotency key, the Payment API returns the first result on the second request instead of charging again.

flashcards.q: What is the minimum protection when you call another system?
flashcards.a: A timeout, being safe to retry (idempotency), and a plan for what happens on failure.
flashcards.more: Without a timeout, a slow system holds your threads and slows you down too. In Symfony HttpClient, `timeout` limits silence and `max_duration` limits the whole request.

flashcards.q: Why move a step like an email out of the request and into a queue?
flashcards.a: If the email is slow or fails, the main job isn't held up, and the queue retries by itself.
flashcards.more: Separating a step that is not a condition of the main job is a typical result of a design review. When you dispatch a message in Symfony Messenger, a worker does the job later and the user doesn't wait.

flashcards.q: What does a good review comment contain?
flashcards.a: A question, a risk and a suggestion, all three, aimed at the design and not the person.
flashcards.more: Saying "this is wrong" puts the author on the defensive. A question like "what happens if it is pressed twice?" lets them see the gap themselves. Adding the risk and a suggestion steers the talk toward a solution.

flashcards.q: The payment API times out. Do you mark the order paid or failed?
flashcards.a: Neither. The outcome is unknown, so keep it pending, then retry with the same Idempotency-Key or check the status.
flashcards.more: A timeout only says that we stopped waiting, not that the charge didn't happen. Marking it failed risks a customer who paid and got nothing; marking it paid risks the opposite. A pending state plus a safe retry (same key) or a status check settles it without a second charge.

flashcards.q: What is a pre-mortem?
flashcards.a: Assuming before the project starts that it has already failed, then working out together why.
flashcards.more: A post-mortem happens after the death; a pre-mortem happens before. Treating failure as having happened lets people voice their fears openly. At the end, each big risk gets one owner and one remedy.

flashcards.q: What is hexagonal architecture (ports and adapters)?
flashcards.a: Business rules sit in the middle, and outside equipment (database, HTTP, SMS) connects through adapters that fulfill interfaces (ports).
flashcards.more: Like a phone's USB-C port: the phone decides its port, and outside chargers are built to fit it. The rules don't know which database is used or who sends the SMS. Dependencies point from outside in.

flashcards.q: What is a port, and what is an adapter?
flashcards.a: A port is an interface written by the inner rules. An adapter is a class that fulfills that interface and talks to outside equipment.
flashcards.more: Example: `OrderRepository` is a port and `DoctrineOrderRepository` is its adapter. `CustomerNotifier` is another port, with `SmsCustomerNotifier` as its adapter. One port can have several adapters (a real one and an in-memory one).

flashcards.q: What is dependency inversion?
flashcards.a: The inner rules don't depend on outer classes; they define an interface, and the outer classes depend on that interface.
flashcards.more: Normally the rules would call the database class, and so depend on it. Here the rules write an interface and the Doctrine adapter fulfills it, so the arrow turns around to point from outside in. More in [[thinking/hexagonal/ports-adapters|ports and adapters]].

flashcards.q: How do you connect an interface to its implementation in Symfony?
flashcards.a: Put `#[AsAlias(Interface::class)]` on the implementing class; autowiring then supplies it whenever that interface is requested.
flashcards.more: With only one implementation Symfony can autowire the interface on its own, but `#[AsAlias]` makes the intent explicit. With several implementations, choose with `#[Target]` or a separate alias.

flashcards.q: What does hexagonal architecture cost, and when is it not worth it?
flashcards.a: Every outside thing needs an interface plus an adapter, so there are more classes. It pays off with complex rules or changing vendors, not plain CRUD.
flashcards.more: In the confirm-order example, one tangled service became two ports, two adapters and a use case. That is a fair price when rules are complex or you may switch vendors, and wasted effort in a small CRUD app.

flashcards.q: Why are business rules easier to test in hexagonal architecture?
flashcards.a: An in-memory fake of a port lets you run the rules with no database or network, so the test finishes in milliseconds.
flashcards.more: `InMemoryOrderRepository` keeps orders in an array, and `SpyNotifier` just remembers whom it was asked to notify. Hand those two to the use case and the whole rule runs. The real adapters are tested separately in integration tests.

flashcards.q: What has to change when you switch vendors in hexagonal architecture?
flashcards.a: Only a new adapter class (or the DSN). The rules, the use case and the rule tests stay as they are.
flashcards.more: Switching SMS vendors means installing a new Notifier bridge and changing the DSN in `.env`. `Order`, `ConfirmOrderHandler` and the rule tests stay exactly as they were.

flashcards.q: When is a port called "leaky"?
flashcards.a: When equipment names creep into the port's methods or types, such as a QueryBuilder or a vendor's statuses.
flashcards.more: That tangles the inner rules with the equipment again. A good port is named in business language: `awaitingPaymentSince()`, not `QueryBuilder`. How the query runs is the adapter's secret.

flashcards.q: What is a ubiquitous language?
flashcards.a: One shared vocabulary for business people and developers, the same in conversation, in documents and in class and method names.
flashcards.more: Writing `cancelByCustomer()` instead of `setStatus(3)` lets a business person read the code and spot a mistake. Misunderstandings shrink and newcomers learn faster. Take the words from the business people; don't invent them yourself.

flashcards.q: How do you turn "when the customer cancels, give store credit" into code?
flashcards.a: Give that sentence its own method in the business's words, such as `cancelByCustomer()`, and put the rule inside it instead of a status number.
flashcards.more: `cancelByCustomer()` and `cancelByUs()` replace `setStatus(3)`. Each one is followed by its own step, credit or refund, so a wrong refund looks wrong at a glance. Do it gradually: add the new method, move callers one by one, then delete the setter.

flashcards.q: What is a bounded context?
flashcards.a: A boundary inside which every word has exactly one meaning and there is exactly one model.
flashcards.more: The same "order" is a bill in Sales, a cooking list in Kitchen and a packet in Delivery. Giving each its own boundary (often its own folder or module) and its own class prevents one huge, confusing model.

flashcards.q: How do bounded contexts talk to each other?
flashcards.a: Through ids, APIs or events, never by reaching into each other's database tables or inner classes.
flashcards.more: A boundary works only if it can't be breached from outside. When Sales publishes an "order placed" event, Kitchen listens and builds its own cooking list in its own language. More in [[messaging/events-vs-commands/cashier-does-everything|events and commands]].

flashcards.q: What does splitting into bounded contexts cost, and when is it not worth it?
flashcards.a: Some data lives in two places and you write hand-off code between contexts. With one team and one meaning per word, a single model is simpler.
flashcards.more: Sales and Kitchen both know an order id and the dish names, and an event carries them across. That is a small price when the meanings really differ. In a small app where every word means one thing, it is just extra code.

flashcards.q: What is the main difference between an entity and a value object?
flashcards.a: An entity has an identity (id) and stays the same when its data changes. A value object has no identity: equal values mean they are the same.
flashcards.more: A Customer entity keeps the same id and is the same person even if the name changes. A Money value object is interchangeable: $500 is $500. Value objects are usually immutable.

flashcards.q: Why store money in cents as an int, or as a Money object, instead of a float?
flashcards.a: Because floats give slightly wrong results (0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3), which is unacceptable for money.
flashcards.more: Integers in cents keep addition and subtraction exact. A Money value object also carries the currency, and throws an exception if you try to add different currencies.

flashcards.q: What goes wrong with `(int) (19.99 * 100)` in PHP?
flashcards.a: It gives 1998, not 1999. The float 19.99 is not exact, so a cent disappears. Keep money as integer cents from the start.
flashcards.more: One lost cent per sale looks harmless, but over 100,000 sales it is $1,000, and no error is ever raised. A Money object built from whole cents never does this conversion.

flashcards.q: What are an aggregate and an aggregate root?
flashcards.a: An aggregate is a cluster of classes that change together and obey the rules together. The root is the cluster's only door.
flashcards.more: Order is the root and OrderLine is an inner part. Outside code never changes OrderLine directly; it goes through Order's methods (`addLine`). The repository exists only for the root.

flashcards.q: What is an invariant, and how does an aggregate protect it?
flashcards.a: An invariant is a rule that must always be true. The aggregate root checks it inside its own methods and keeps its setters hidden.
flashcards.more: Example: "an order has at most 20 items". `addLine()` checks this, so no route lets a 21st item in. When the rule is scattered around controllers, it breaks the moment one person forgets.

flashcards.q: What is event-driven architecture?
flashcards.a: When the work is done you just announce the fact (an event); whoever needs it listens and does their own job.
flashcards.more: Like a notice board: the headmaster pins up the announcement and doesn't know who will read it. So the announcer's job stays simple, adding a listener means no change to its code, and one listener breaking doesn't stop it.

flashcards.q: What is the main difference between an event and a command?
flashcards.a: An event is a fact about the past (OrderPlaced); a command is an instruction about the future (PlaceOrder), with one specific recipient.
flashcards.more: An event doesn't force anyone to do anything; whoever wants to hears it. A command tells one specific handler to do a job, and may expect a result. More in [[messaging/events-vs-commands/cashier-does-everything|event vs command]].

flashcards.q: What does CQRS mean?
flashcards.a: Splitting Command (write) and Query (read) into separate models, so each can be shaped for its own job.
flashcards.more: In the library, the checkout log (rules) and the catalog (speed) are separate. In CQRS too, the write model enforces rules, and the read model is fast and flat. The simplest form: same database, but separate command handlers and query classes.

flashcards.q: Are CQRS and event sourcing the same thing?
flashcards.a: No. CQRS splits reading from writing; event sourcing keeps the list of events as the real data. You can have either without the other.
flashcards.more: Many people use them together, which is why they get mixed up. But CQRS works on an ordinary SQL database too, and an event-driven system doesn't need event sourcing. Each has its own price and its own benefits. More in [[workflows/event-sourcing/why-is-it-200|event sourcing]].

flashcards.q: What are the main costs of an event-driven system?
flashcards.a: Harder debugging (who is listening to what), eventual consistency, the risk of events arriving twice, and the care needed when changing an event's shape.
flashcards.more: The result of one job is now spread across several places, so logs and tracing are essential. Handlers must be idempotent, because a message can arrive twice. Change an event's fields and its listeners may break.

flashcards.q: What does it mean for a CQRS read model to "lag behind"?
flashcards.a: Right after a write the read model may not be updated yet; it catches up a few moments later. This is called eventual consistency.
flashcards.more: Right after an order is placed, the new order may not yet appear in the list. You handle it in the UI, by showing "processing" or by showing the user their own write straight away. Be careful where an instantly correct answer is needed, such as a balance.

flashcards.q: How do you keep commands and events apart in Symfony Messenger?
flashcards.a: With two separate buses: command.bus and event.bus. The event bus gets `allow_no_handlers: true`.
flashcards.more: Write `#[AsMessageHandler(bus: 'event.bus')]` on a handler and it attaches to that bus. Inject `MessageBusInterface $eventBus` and Symfony supplies the event.bus. An event bus with no listeners is not a mistake.

flashcards.q: What can go wrong between saving an order and dispatching its event?
flashcards.a: If the server dies between the two, the order exists but the event is never sent, so no stock, no email, and no error.
flashcards.more: The line that failed never ran, so nothing is logged. The fix is to store the event in the same database transaction as the order, then let a worker deliver it.

flashcards.q: How does Messenger avoid losing an event when the server crashes?
flashcards.a: The `doctrine_transaction` middleware plus a Doctrine transport store the event in the same transaction as the data. A worker delivers it later.
flashcards.more: The price is at-least-once delivery, so handlers must be idempotent. It works because the queue shares the database connection; with RabbitMQ or SQS you need a real outbox table and a relay. If losing an event is harmless, plain dispatch is fine.

flashcards.q: What is the concrete pain that CQRS fixes on a list page?
flashcards.a: Building 20 full Order objects costs 1 query plus one per order for the lines: 21 queries. A flat read table answers in 1.
flashcards.more: The write model is shaped for rules, not for display, so reading through it is slow and heavy. The read side skips the objects and reads one pre-arranged row per order. The price is keeping that table in step, with a short lag.

flashcards.q: What is the C4 model?
flashcards.a: Four levels for drawing software architecture: Context, Container, Component, Code. It works like zooming a map.
flashcards.more: Each level answers a different question, and each diagram holds just one level. For most teams the Context and Container diagrams are enough. Simon Brown popularized the approach.

flashcards.q: What does the C4 Context diagram show, and for whom?
flashcards.a: Our system, its users and the outside systems. Relationships, not technology. For everyone, including non-technical people.
flashcards.more: For an online shop, the Context diagram would hold the customer, the admin, the payment gateway and the SMS vendor. The internal technology isn't written here. This is the picture a newcomer or a PM sees first.

flashcards.q: What does "Container" mean in C4?
flashcards.a: A separately running and deployed part: the Vue app, the Symfony API, the database, a worker. It doesn't have to be a Docker container.
flashcards.more: The name is confusing. Here a container is any separate part that holds data or runs code. Each box carries a name, a responsibility and a technology, and each arrow carries a protocol.

flashcards.q: When should you draw a sequence diagram?
flashcards.a: When order and failure branches matter: checkout, retries, timeouts, webhooks.
flashcards.more: A C4 picture has no time in it, so it can't answer "what happens if the money is taken and then we time out?" One diagram per scenario, covering the happy and the failing path, with real API names on the messages. Mermaid can live in the repository as text.

flashcards.q: What is an ADR (Architecture Decision Record)?
flashcards.a: A short record of one big decision: the context, the decision, the alternatives rejected and the consequences.
flashcards.more: It lives in the repository with a number, like `docs/adr/0007-...md`. When someone asks "why is it like this?", the answer is there. Write them only for hard-to-reverse or contested decisions.

flashcards.q: What happens to an ADR when the decision changes?
flashcards.a: The old ADR is not edited. A new ADR is written, and the old one's status becomes "Superseded by ...".
flashcards.more: Like a court ruling, the history is not erased, so someone in the future can see when and why a decision changed. The statuses are: Proposed, Accepted, Superseded (or Deprecated).

flashcards.q: Why is it better to keep diagrams and ADRs beside the code in the repository?
flashcards.a: Because the diagram or decision is updated and reviewed in the same pull request as the code change, so it goes stale less.
flashcards.more: Nobody remembers a wiki picture when changing code, and within a few years it lies. As Mermaid or Structurizr DSL files, you can see diffs, validate them in CI, and have GitHub render the picture for you.

flashcards.q: Does keeping a diagram in the repository guarantee it stays true?
flashcards.a: No. CI can check that the file is valid, not that it is true. The reviewer must still ask: did this change touch the picture?
flashcards.more: The repository only makes the fix cheap: the picture changes in the same pull request as the code, and the diff shows it. Someone still has to look. Add the question to the pull request checklist so it is asked every time.
